blocks.text: The 12 V relay that switches a pneumatic valve survives millions of cycles only because of a 10-cent diode wired backwards across its coil. Remove that diode and each turn-off sends a voltage spike of hundreds of volts into the transistor driving it. The diode is a one-way valve for current, and that single property gives us rectifiers, protection and indicator lamps.

blocks.markdown: An ideal **diode** conducts current from **anode** to **cathode** when forward-biased and blocks current when reverse-biased. A real silicon diode needs a **forward voltage drop** $V_f\approx0.7$ V (typical; about 0.3 V for a Schottky diode) before it conducts appreciably, and once conducting its voltage stays close to $V_f$. Light-emitting diodes (LEDs) work the same way but with a larger $V_f$ that depends on colour: typically 1.8 to 2.2 V for red and green, and about 3 V for blue and white.

blocks.title: Constant-drop diode model
blocks.text: Forward-biased: the diode is a fixed voltage source $V_f$ in the direction of conduction (current can only flow anode to cathode). Reverse-biased: open circuit (zero current), up to the breakdown voltage. This model is accurate enough for most switching and rectifier calculations.

blocks.markdown: **Half-wave rectifier.** Put a diode in series with a load resistor and drive it from an AC source $v_{in}=V_p\sin\omega t$, where $V_p=\sqrt2\,V_{rms}$ is the peak voltage. During the positive half-cycle the diode conducts once $v_{in}$ exceeds $V_f$, and the load sees $v_{in}-V_f$. In the negative half-cycle the diode blocks and the load voltage is zero. The output is a train of positive humps, with peak $V_p-V_f$, that is clipped slightly at its base.

blocks.caption: Peak of the rectified output and conduction angle per cycle (the diode conducts only while v_in > V_f)

blocks.title: Half-wave rectifier output
blocks.prompt: A transformer secondary gives 12.0 V rms. It feeds a silicon diode ($V_f=0.7$ V) in series with a 220 ohm load. Find the peak output voltage and the peak load current.

steps.text: Subtract the diode drop at the peak.

blocks.answer: Peak load voltage 16.3 V and peak load current 74 mA. The diode must also withstand a reverse voltage of about $V_p = 17$ V during the negative half-cycle.

blocks.markdown: **LED current limiting.** An LED's voltage is nearly constant above $V_f$, so connecting it directly to a supply would let the current rise without limit and destroy it. A series resistor $R$ takes up the remaining voltage. Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop gives the design equation below.

blocks.caption: Series resistor for supply V_s, LED forward voltage V_f and chosen forward current I_F

blocks.title: Choosing an LED resistor
blocks.prompt: A red LED ($V_f=2.0$ V) is to run at 15 mA from a 5.0 V supply. Find $R$, choose a standard value and recompute the actual current.

steps.text: The nearest standard value above is 220 ohm; recompute the current.

blocks.answer: Use 220 ohm, which gives 13.6 mA. Rounding up is the safe direction, since it only reduces current.

blocks.markdown: **Flyback (freewheel) diode.** An inductive load such as a relay coil or solenoid stores energy $\tfrac12LI^2$. If the switch opens, the current $I$ cannot drop to zero instantly, so the coil produces a large voltage $v=L\,di/dt$ of reversed polarity that can exceed the switch's rating. A diode connected **across the coil, cathode toward the positive supply**, is reverse-biased in normal operation and does nothing. When the switch opens, the coil's reversed voltage forward-biases the diode, which gives the current a path to circulate and decay. The coil voltage is clamped near $-V_f$.

rows: Clamps the inductive spike; passes decaying coil current
blocks.caption: Common roles of diodes in mechatronic circuits

items: Silicon $V_f\approx0.7$ V, Schottky $\approx0.3$ V, LED about 1.8 to 3 V (typical values).
Half-wave output peak is $V_p-V_f$; conduction angle is slightly less than 180 degrees.
The LED resistor is $R=(V_s-V_f)/I_F$, rounded to a standard value that gives a safe current.
A flyback diode must be rated for the full coil current at turn-off.

blocks.title: Flyback diode polarity
blocks.text: Fitted the wrong way round, the diode conducts the full supply current whenever the coil is switched on, creating a short circuit across the supply. Cathode to the positive side, anode to the switch side.

points: A real diode conducts only above $V_f$; a half-wave rectifier's output peaks at $V_p-V_f$ with $V_p=\sqrt2V_{rms}$.
A flyback diode across an inductive load gives the coil current a path at turn-off and clamps the voltage spike.

questions.stem: A 3.3 V supply drives an LED with $V_f=1.8$ V at 10 mA through a series resistor. Which resistor value is required?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this uses the full 3.3 V across the resistor and ignores the LED drop.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this uses V_f/I = 1.8/0.010, dividing the LED voltage rather than the resistor voltage.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is 1.5/0.1, a decimal slip by a factor of ten in the current.

questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's voltage law gives $V_R=3.3-1.8=1.5$ V across the resistor. Then $R=V_R/I=1.5/0.010=150$ ohm.

questions.stem: A sinusoidal source of 10 V peak drives a silicon diode ($V_f=0.7$ V) in series with a resistor (half-wave rectifier). What is the peak voltage across the resistor?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this ignores the diode drop.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this adds the drop instead of subtracting it.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this subtracts the drop twice, as if there were two conducting diodes.

questions.explanation: The diode drops $V_f$ whenever it conducts, so the load peak is $V_p-V_f=10-0.7=9.3$ V.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a flyback diode across a relay coil?

options.text: To give the coil current a path when the switch opens, limiting the voltage spike
To increase the coil's pull-in force
To rectify the AC supply to the coil
To reduce the current when the coil is energised

questions.correctOptionText: To give the coil current a path when the switch opens, limiting the voltage spike

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it conducts the decaying inductor current and clamps the voltage.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the diode is reverse-biased while the coil is energised and has no effect on force.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the supply is DC; rectification is not involved.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the diode carries no current while the coil is on.

questions.explanation: An inductor resists a change in current, so opening the switch would force a huge $L\,di/dt$ voltage. The flyback diode conducts and lets the current decay safely.

questions.stem: A relay coil is powered from +12 V through a low-side transistor switch (coil between +12 V and the transistor). Which is the correct flyback diode connection?

options.text: Cathode to +12 V, anode to the transistor side of the coil
Anode to +12 V, cathode to the transistor side of the coil
In series with the coil, anode to +12 V
Across the transistor, anode to ground

questions.correctOptionText: Cathode to +12 V, anode to the transistor side of the coil

distractorRationale.a: Correct: reverse-biased while the coil is on; conducts when the coil voltage reverses.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is forward-biased and would short the supply to the transistor node.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: a series diode would block the reverse current path it must provide.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this does not clamp the inductive kick safely and is not placed across the coil.

questions.explanation: In normal operation the transistor node is near 0 V and the diode's cathode is at +12 V, so it is reverse-biased. At turn-off the coil end at the transistor swings above +12 V, forward-biasing the diode and providing a path for the current.

questions.stem: A 5.0 V peak sine wave drives a silicon diode ($V_f=0.7$ V) in a half-wave rectifier. For approximately what fraction of each full cycle does the diode conduct?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it conducts while 5 sin(theta) > 0.7, i.e. 8.05 to 171.95 degrees = 163.9 degrees, 45.5 % of 360.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is the ideal diode case with V_f = 0.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this is 100 % minus 14 %, which confuses the blocked fraction.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is V_f/V_p, not a time fraction.

questions.explanation: Conduction starts when $5\sin\theta=0.7$, i.e. $\theta=\arcsin(0.14)=8.05^\circ$, and ends at $171.95^\circ$. That is $163.9^\circ$ of $360^\circ$, or 45.5 %.

questions.stem: A white LED ($V_f=3.1$ V typical) is to run at 20 mA from a 12 V supply. What series resistance (in ohms) is needed?
questions.explanation: The resistor must drop $12-3.1=8.9$ V at 20 mA, so $R=8.9/0.020=445$ ohm. A standard 470 ohm part would give about 18.9 mA.

questions.stem: A green LED ($V_f=2.2$ V) is connected with a 330 ohm series resistor to a 5.0 V supply. What current (in mA) does it carry?
questions.explanation: The resistor drops $5.0-2.2=2.8$ V, so $I=2.8/330=8.5$ mA. This is a safe, comfortably bright level for a small indicator LED.

questions.stem: A transformer secondary of 18.0 V rms feeds a silicon diode ($V_f=0.7$ V) and a 47 ohm resistor in series (half-wave rectifier). What is the peak load current, in amperes?
questions.explanation: The peak source voltage is $\sqrt2\times18.0=25.46$ V. After the diode drop the peak load voltage is $24.76$ V, so $I_{peak}=24.76/47=0.527$ A.

questions.stem: A 24 V solenoid (inductance 0.2 H, carrying 0.5 A) is switched by a transistor. Explain what happens when the transistor turns off with and without a flyback diode. Include the energy stored in the coil.
markingGuide: States stored energy 0.5 L I^2 = 25 mJ
States an inductor opposes sudden current change: v = L di/dt
Without diode, current is forced to fall fast so the coil voltage spikes far above 24 V, possibly destroying the transistor
With diode across the coil, cathode to supply, the diode conducts the decaying current
Voltage clamped to about the supply plus V_f at the transistor node, energy dissipated in coil resistance and diode
questions.explanation: The coil stores $\tfrac12LI^2=0.5\times0.2\times0.5^2=25$ mJ. Without a diode the transistor tries to cut the current abruptly, so $v=L\,di/dt$ becomes very large and may exceed the transistor's rating. With a flyback diode the coil current continues through it and decays slowly, and the transistor sees only about the supply voltage plus one diode drop.

questions.stem: Describe and sketch (in words, giving key voltages and angles) the output of a half-wave rectifier driven by a 6 V peak, 50 Hz sine through a silicon diode with $V_f=0.7$ V into a resistor. State the peak output, the time the diode conducts per cycle, and the peak reverse voltage across the diode.
markingGuide: Output is zero during negative half-cycles
Diode conducts only when v_in > 0.7 V: starts at about 6.7 degrees and stops at about 173.3 degrees
Conduction time per cycle approx 166.6/360 x 20 ms = about 9.3 ms (less than a half period of 10 ms)
Peak reverse voltage across diode about 6 V (the source peak) when load is purely resistive
questions.explanation: The load peak is $6-0.7=5.3$ V and the output is zero in the negative half-cycle. Conduction starts when $6\sin\theta=0.7$, i.e. at $6.7^\circ$, and ends at $173.3^\circ$, giving $166.6^\circ$ or about 9.3 ms of each 20 ms period. The reverse voltage across the diode reaches about 6 V.
